info.title: RoleBlank OS API
info.summary: The HTTP contract of the RoleBlank OS backend.
info.description:
**This is an internal company system. The API is not public.**

RoleBlank OS is the operating system of a single company: one organisation, one
database, no tenants. It is not a product sold to third parties and there is no
public sign-up. Every deployment is expected to sit behind the company's own
network boundary, and nothing in this document should be read as an invitation to
expose it to the open internet.

There are exactly two kinds of human principal:

* `INTERNAL` — company staff. The whole surface below is potentially reachable,
  subject to permissions and scope.
* `CLIENT` — an external human at a customer business. A `CLIENT` principal may
  reach **only** the `/api/v1/client-portal/*` endpoints. Every other route is
  refused before any grant is consulted, because the two permissions a `CLIENT`
  may hold at all are `client.portal.projects.read` and `client.portal.tasks.read`.
  A `CLIENT` that asks for an object it cannot see is answered `404`, never `403`:
  a refusal must not confirm that the object exists.

### Reading this document against the code

Every operation carries three vendor extensions, the first two taken verbatim from
`ROUTE_TABLE` in `backend/src/routes.rs`:

* `x-required-permission` — the permission code the handler demands, or `null`.
* `x-requires-step-up` — whether a second factor verified within the step-up window
  (600 seconds by default) is additionally required.
* `x-principal-types` — which kinds of principal can reach the route at all.
  `["ANONYMOUS"]` is the unauthenticated surface; `["INTERNAL"]` is company staff
  only, because the permission's envelope is `INTERNAL` and no `CLIENT` may ever
  hold it; `["INTERNAL","CLIENT"]` covers the session-scoped endpoints (logout,
  MFA, own password, own sessions) and the client portal. A `CLIENT` that calls an
  `["INTERNAL"]` route is answered `404`, never `403`.

The same registry is published as machine-readable data in `api/endpoints.json`, and
in code as `backend/src/platform/http/endpoints.rs`, which is the single place a
route pattern is written down for callers inside the backend.

`backend/tests/openapi_contract.rs` fails the build when this file and that table
disagree, in either direction. Documenting an endpoint that does not exist is as
much a failure as shipping one that is not documented.

### Errors

Every error is RFC 9457 `application/problem+json` with a stable SCREAMING_SNAKE
`code`. **Machine clients branch on `code` and never on prose**: `title` and
`detail` are human text and may be reworded at any time. `detail` never carries an
internal fact — no SQL, no backtrace, no file path, no hostname.

There is deliberately no `422`. A payload that parses as JSON but fails validation
is `400` with `code: VALIDATION_FAILED` and a `errors` array of field errors; the
server has one bad-request status, not two.

### Conventions

* Timestamps are RFC 3339 strings; plain dates are ISO calendar dates.
* Collections are cursor-paginated. There is no offset pagination anywhere: an
  offset lets a client turn a cheap endpoint into an expensive one by incrementing
  a number.
* `sort` is an allowlist per endpoint, never a column name that reaches SQL.
* Mutating requests on versioned resources carry `version`, and a stale one is
  `409 VERSION_CONFLICT`. An absent `version` is a validation error, not a blind
  overwrite.

tags.name: System
tags.description:
Liveness, readiness, metrics and the minimal authenticated environment description.
The three probes are anonymous by necessity and answer with a closed vocabulary that
cannot carry runtime detail.

tags.name: Bootstrap
tags.description:
One-time creation of the system owner.

There is deliberately **no ownership-transfer endpoint**. `system_ownership` is a
singleton row that database triggers refuse to update or delete unconditionally, with
no exception for administrators. Any code path that could legitimately move ownership
is a code path that could be abused to steal it, so ownership recovery is an offline
procedure performed by the schema owner, not an API.

tags.name: Authentication
tags.description:
Sessions, tokens, password changes and password resets. Tokens are opaque server-side
session tokens, never JWTs.

tags.name: MFA
tags.description:
TOTP enrolment, verification and recovery codes. The endpoints in this tag are the
only ones a password-only session may reach, together with `GET /api/v1/auth/me` —
that is the entire purpose of the pending state.

tags.name: Registration
tags.description:
Self-registration, when the deployment has it switched on. It can only ever create a
`CLIENT` principal in `PENDING` status.

tags.name: Users
tags.description:
Reading and administering user accounts.

There is deliberately **no user-delete endpoint**, and the runtime database role holds
no `DELETE` grant on `users` at all. Users are archived, never erased, so that
historical references and the meaning of the audit log survive. There is also no `POST
/api/v1/users`: an account comes into existence only through invitation acceptance,
self-registration, or bootstrap.

tags.name: Invitations
tags.description: Creating, listing and revoking invitations, and the anonymous endpoint that redeems one.

tags.name: Authorization
tags.description:
The permission catalogue, roles, role assignment and per-user permission overrides.
Everything that grants authority is behind step-up.

tags.name: Departments
tags.description: Internal company structure. Flat by design.

tags.name: Clients
tags.description:
External client accounts and their memberships. A client account is a business; a
client membership is the link that gives one external human visibility, and it grants
nothing until it is activated.

tags.name: Projects
tags.description:
Projects, their internal members, and the shares that make a project visible to a
client account.

There is deliberately **no file-upload endpoint** anywhere in this API. Accepting
user-supplied files brings content-type sniffing, antivirus, storage-quota and
stored-XSS problems that this system has no requirement to take on; document exchange
happens outside it.

tags.name: Tasks
tags.description:
Tasks, their assignees, and the per-task `client_visible` flag that is the only thing
which can expose a task externally.

tags.name: Client Portal
tags.description:
The complete surface an external `CLIENT` principal may reach. Four read-only
operations, returning strictly reduced projections. Nothing here mutates anything.

tags.name: Settings
tags.description:
System settings and feature flags. Both are versioned and both distinguish
security-sensitive keys.

tags.name: Audit
tags.description:
Reading and verifying the append-only audit log.

There is deliberately **no audit-write endpoint**. Audit rows are written only by the
server as a side effect of the operation being audited. The table refuses `UPDATE`,
`DELETE` and `TRUNCATE` at the database level with no actor-dependent branch, because
an administrator who can rewrite history can erase their own escalation.

get.description:
Reports that the process is alive; it answers as long as the server is running
and does not touch the database or any other dependency. Anonymous by necessity
— an orchestrator's probe carries no credentials — so the body is one of exactly
two fixed documents and carries no runtime detail: no version, no hostname, no
dependency name. There is no failure mode other than the process being
unreachable, in which case nothing answers at all. Do not use it for readiness:
it keeps answering `200` while every dependency is down.

Reports whether this instance is willing to take traffic, which includes
establishing that its dependencies are reachable. Anonymous by necessity, and
answered from the same closed vocabulary as the liveness probe: a failing
dependency is never named, so the body says only `ready` or `not_ready`. A `503`
means take this instance out of rotation; a `200` means it may serve. Load
balancers should poll this route rather than `/health/live`.

200.description: The instance is ready to serve traffic.

503.description: The instance is not ready. The body says only `not_ready`.

get.description:
Prometheus text exposition for this instance, as `text/plain` rather than JSON.
It is anonymous because scrapers do not authenticate, which makes it the one
route whose protection is entirely operational: deploy it behind a network
boundary. Series are labelled by route *pattern* and never by a concrete path,
so label cardinality stays bounded and a caller cannot inflate the metric store
by walking UUIDs. It is rate limited like everything else on the anonymous
surface.

get.summary: Whether the system has an owner yet
get.description:
Says whether the system already has an owner, as a single boolean and
deliberately nothing else. Anonymous by necessity: before the owner exists there
is nobody to authenticate as, so every extra field here would be free
reconnaissance for an unauthenticated caller. It is rate limited, and exceeding
the limit is `429 RATE_LIMITED` with a `Retry-After` header. Use it to decide
whether to show a bootstrap screen or a login screen.

post.description:
Creates the single ROOT owner and closes bootstrap permanently. Anonymous, but
gated on the out-of-band operator secret supplied in `bootstrap_secret`, which
is compared in constant time; a wrong secret is refused and the route is rate
limited. It succeeds at most once for the life of a deployment — a second
attempt is `409 SYSTEM_ALREADY_INITIALIZED` — and there is deliberately no
ownership-transfer endpoint to undo it, because any code path that can move
ownership can be abused to steal it. No session and no token is returned: the
owner must log in through the ordinary authentication path and enrol a second
factor, so bootstrap cannot mint a privileged session by itself.

post.summary: Exchange an email and password for a session
post.description:
Exchanges an email and password for an access token and a refresh token, both of
which are opaque server-side session handles rather than JWTs. Anonymous and
rate limited, and reachable by internal staff and external client users alike.
Every failure mode — unknown account, wrong password, suspended user, archived
user — renders as the same `401 AUTHENTICATION_FAILED`, and the unknown-account
path still performs a full Argon2id verification so that the timing matches; any
distinction here would be an account-enumeration oracle. When the account
requires MFA the response still carries tokens but sets `mfa_required: true`,
and that session may reach only the MFA endpoints, `GET /api/v1/auth/me` and
logout until it verifies. `Idempotency-Key` is deliberately not honoured here:
replaying a login is not a safe thing to make idempotent.

post.summary: Rotate an access token using a refresh token
post.description:
Exchanges a refresh token for a fresh access and refresh pair; both tokens
rotate on every call. It needs no bearer header — the refresh token in the body
is the credential — and it is reachable by internal and client principals alike.
Presenting a refresh token that has already been redeemed is treated as theft
rather than as a race: the entire session family is revoked,
`AUTH.REFRESH_REUSE_DETECTED` is audited, and the response is `401
AUTHENTICATION_FAILED`. Clients must therefore serialise their refreshes,
because two concurrent calls will end the session. The absolute session lifetime
(30 days by default) is never extended by refreshing.

Revokes exactly the session presenting the bearer token, and nothing else. Any
authenticated principal may call it — internal or external, and a session that
has not yet completed MFA may call it too — and no permission is required. It is
idempotent in effect: replaying it with an already revoked token simply fails
authentication with `401`, and the session stays revoked. Success is `204` with
no body.

post.summary: Revoke every session belonging to the caller
post.description:
Revokes every session belonging to the caller, including the one making the
request, and reports how many were revoked. Any authenticated principal may call
it, internal or external, and no permission is required; it is the self-service
answer to "I think my account is compromised". It does not change the password,
so a caller who suspects theft should also call `POST
/api/v1/auth/password/change`. The caller's own token is dead as soon as the
call returns, so a repeat attempt with it is `401`.

get.summary: The calling principal and its capability hints
get.description:
Returns the calling principal and, for a fully authenticated session, its
effective capabilities. Any session may call it, including one that has
authenticated with a password but not yet completed MFA — this route and the MFA
endpoints are the entire pending-state surface — and no permission is required.
The two cases return structurally different documents: a pending session gets a
physically smaller projection with no `capabilities` and no `is_root`, because a
session that cannot call a business endpoint has no business learning which ones
it would be allowed to call. `capabilities` is a hint for hiding buttons and
never a security boundary; the backend re-derives every decision on every
request, and `security_version` increments whenever a privilege change means the
client should re-fetch.

Lists the caller's own live sessions so that a user can review where they are
logged in. Any authenticated principal may call it and no permission is
required; there is deliberately no endpoint for reading somebody else's
sessions. The `*_hint` fields are recognition aids for a human and are never
consulted for authorisation. It is not cursor-paginated, because a single user's
live session set is bounded; revoked and expired sessions are not listed.

delete.summary: Revoke one of the caller's own sessions
delete.description:
Revokes one of the caller's own sessions by id, which is how a user kills a
session on a device they no longer have. Any authenticated principal may call it
and no permission is required, but the session must belong to the caller. A
session id belonging to another user yields `404`, not `403`: the refusal must
not confirm that the session exists. Revoking the session that is making the
request is allowed and simply logs the caller out; the response is `204` either
way.

post.description:
Changes the caller's own password, requiring the current password in the same
request as proof of possession. Any authenticated principal may call it and no
permission is required; there is no endpoint anywhere for setting somebody
else's password. A wrong current password is `401 AUTHENTICATION_FAILED`, and a
new password that fails the strength policy is `400 VALIDATION_FAILED` with the
offending field named in `errors`. On success every *other* session of the user
is revoked, so the caller keeps its own tokens but every other device must log
in again.

Starts a password reset by emailing a single-use token to the address supplied.
Anonymous and rate limited, because a reset form has to work for somebody who
cannot log in. The `202` body is a fixed constant with no variable field at all
— byte for byte identical for an existing address, a non-existent address and a
structurally invalid one — and it is a struct with nothing to vary precisely so
that no later edit can make it depend on the account. Neither the response nor
its timing distinguishes the three cases, so it cannot be used to enumerate
accounts.

post.summary: Complete a password reset with a token
post.description:
Completes a password reset by presenting the emailed token together with the new
password. Anonymous and rate limited; the token is the only credential. The
token travels in the body and never in the URL, because a URL is logged by
proxies, kept in browser history and forwarded in `Referer` — a token found in
the query string is rejected with `400 BAD_REQUEST`. An expired, already used or
unknown token is `401 AUTHENTICATION_FAILED`, undifferentiated as everywhere
else. On success the user's sessions are revoked and the response is `204`.

Starts TOTP enrolment and returns the shared secret together with its
`otpauth://` URI. Reachable by any session including one that is still MFA-
pending, since a user who is required to enrol must be able to do so before
completing MFA; no permission is required. This is the one response in the API
that carries a secret, and it carries it exactly once — at rest the factor holds
only XChaCha20-Poly1305 ciphertext, so the secret can never be read back. The
factor is inert until `POST /api/v1/auth/mfa/totp/activate` succeeds, and
calling setup while an active factor already exists is `409`.

Activates a pending TOTP factor by proving possession of the authenticator with
a current code. Reachable by an MFA-pending session, and no permission is
required. A wrong or replayed code is refused, and there is nothing to activate
if setup was not called first, which is `409`. On success it returns the
recovery-code batch, shown once and only once: only SHA-256 digests are stored,
so the codes cannot be re-read and a lost batch must be regenerated.

post.summary: Complete MFA for a pending session
post.description:
Completes multi-factor authentication for a session that logged in with
`mfa_required: true`. This is the one thing a password-only session exists to
do, so the endpoint accepts an MFA-pending bearer token; no permission is
required. Success lifts the session out of the pending state and opens the step-
up window (600 seconds by default), which is what every step-up-protected
endpoint later checks. A wrong or expired code is `401 AUTHENTICATION_FAILED`,
and codes are single-use within their time step so a replay is refused.

post.summary: Complete MFA with a single-use recovery code
post.description:
Completes MFA with one of the single-use recovery codes issued at enrolment —
the break-glass path for a lost authenticator. Reachable by an MFA-pending
session, and no permission is required. Each code is consumed on use and the
response reports how many remain, so a user can regenerate before running out. A
wrong or already spent code is `401 AUTHENTICATION_FAILED`; exhausting the batch
entirely means an operator must intervene out of band.

post.summary: Issue a fresh batch of recovery codes
post.description:
Issues a fresh batch of recovery codes and invalidates the previous batch in the
same transaction. Requires a fully authenticated session **and** a second factor
verified within the step-up window, otherwise `403 STEP_UP_REQUIRED` carrying
`step_up.window_seconds`; no permission code is involved, because the operation
only ever acts on the caller's own account. The step-up is the entire point: an
attacker holding a live stolen session must not be able to mint themselves a
persistent second factor. The codes are returned once and only their digests are
stored, and there is no factor to regenerate against if MFA is not enrolled
(`409`).

Disables multi-factor authentication for the caller and removes the enrolled
factor. Requires a fully authenticated session behind step-up — `403
STEP_UP_REQUIRED` otherwise — and no permission code, because it acts only on
the caller. It is refused outright for the system owner, for whom MFA cannot be
made optional; that refusal is `403 ROOT_PROTECTED` and is never masked as a
`404`, not even for an external principal. Disabling when nothing is enrolled is
`409`.

get.description:
Says whether self-registration is open and, if it is, that it is of the `client`
kind. Anonymous and rate limited, because a sign-up screen has to render before
anybody has a session. Two fields and nothing more: it must not disclose the
configured mode name, the company, or whether invitations exist. Treat a
negative answer as final — calling `POST /api/v1/registration` anyway is `403`.

post.description:
Submits a self-registration request. Anonymous and rate limited, and available
only while the `registration.mode` setting is `CLIENT_SELF_REGISTRATION`;
otherwise it is `403`. It can only ever create a `CLIENT` principal in `PENDING`
status with no client memberships and therefore no visibility of anything: the
request type has no field for `principal_type`, none for `role_ids` and none for
`status`, so smuggling one is a `400 VALIDATION_FAILED` from deserialisation
before the service is even entered. The `202` body is a fixed constant and does
not reveal whether the address was already registered. Somebody holding
`clients.members.manage` must attach and activate the account before the new
user can see anything at all.

post.summary: Redeem an invitation token and create the account
post.description:
Redeems an invitation token and creates the invitee's account. Anonymous by
necessity — the invitee has no account yet — and the token travels in the body,
never in the path or the query string. The invitee's principal type, department
or client account and role set were fixed by the inviter and are re-validated
against the inviter's own delegation authority at this moment, so a stale
invitation cannot outlive the authority that created it; a failure there is
`403`. An unknown or expired token is `404` and an already redeemed one is
`409`. No session and no token is returned: the new account must log in through
the ordinary path.

get.description:
Lists user accounts, cursor-paginated, with optional `principal_type`, `status`
and `search` filters. Requires `iam.users.read`; a `CLIENT` principal can never
hold that code, because its envelope is `INTERNAL`, so an external caller is
refused before any grant is consulted and is answered `404` rather than `403`. A
narrow permission scope does not become a refusal, it becomes a filtered query,
so a caller with limited reach gets a smaller page instead of an error. `sort`
is an allowlist and an unlisted value is `400` without the rejected string being
echoed back; `limit` outside 1–100 is `400` rather than being silently clamped.

parameters.name: search
parameters.description: Case-insensitive substring over the normalised email and the display name.

get.description:
Reads one user account by id. Requires `iam.users.read`, an `INTERNAL`-only
permission, so a `CLIENT` principal cannot reach this route and receives `404`.
`email_normalized` is deliberately absent from the projection, as is anything
from the `credentials` table — that table is separate precisely so that the
query on the authenticated path cannot return a password hash. An id that does
not exist is `404`; an internal caller lacking the permission on an object that
does exist gets `403`, while the same refusal to an external caller is rendered
as `404`.

patch.description:
Updates a user's own attributes. Requires `iam.users.update` — `INTERNAL` only,
so a `CLIENT` caller sees `404` — and no step-up. Only `display_name` and
`email` are writable here: `principal_type`, `status`, `security_version`,
`mfa_required` and role membership are not fields of this request and cannot be
steered by it, and an unrecognised field is `400` rather than an ignored extra.
`version` is the optimistic-concurrency token and is mandatory — a stale one is
`409 VERSION_CONFLICT` carrying the expected and actual values, and an absent
one is a validation error rather than a blind overwrite. An operation targeting
the system owner is refused with `403 ROOT_PROTECTED`.

post.description:
Suspends a user, revoking every session the subject holds so that the block
takes effect on their next request rather than at token expiry. Requires
`iam.users.suspend`, an `INTERNAL`-only permission, so a `CLIENT` caller sees
`404`; no step-up is required. `version` is mandatory, so a stale read is `409
VERSION_CONFLICT`. It is refused for the system owner with `403 ROOT_PROTECTED`,
which is never masked, and suspending an already suspended or archived account
is `409`.

Returns a suspended account to `ACTIVE`. Requires `iam.users.suspend` — the same
permission that suspends, because the authority to undo a suspension is the same
authority — and no step-up; a `CLIENT` principal cannot hold the code and is
answered `404`. `version` is mandatory and a stale one is `409
VERSION_CONFLICT`. An archived account is not reactivated by this endpoint:
archival is terminal, and that transition is refused with `409`.

Archives a user account. Requires `iam.users.archive` — `INTERNAL` only, so an
external caller sees `404` — together with the mandatory `version`. Archival is
the terminal state and the closest thing to deletion this API offers: there is
no `DELETE /api/v1/users/{id}` and the runtime database role holds no `DELETE`
grant on `users` at all, so the row survives and historical references and audit
meaning survive with it. Archiving the system owner is `403 ROOT_PROTECTED`, and
archiving an already archived account is `409`.

get.description:
Lists invitations, cursor-paginated and optionally filtered by `status`.
Requires `iam.users.invite`, an `INTERNAL`-only permission, so a `CLIENT` caller
is answered `404`; no step-up is required. No projection here carries the
invitation token or its digest — the token exists only in the email that was
sent, and no endpoint anywhere can read it back. `sort` is allowlisted and
`limit` is bounded at 100.

post.description:
Creates an invitation and sends it, which is the only path to an `INTERNAL`
account — there is deliberately no `POST /api/v1/users`. Requires
`iam.users.invite` (`INTERNAL` only, so a `CLIENT` caller sees `404`) and no
step-up, but the requested role set is validated against the inviter's own
authority now and again at acceptance, so an over-reaching invitation is `403
DELEGATION_DENIED` immediately. It honours `Idempotency-Key`: the same key with
the same body replays the stored response, while the same key with a different
body is `409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED` rather than a silently wrong replay. There
is one live invitation per address, so inviting the same person twice is a
deterministic `409`, and the response has no field the token could occupy.

201.description: The invitation was created and an email dispatched.

delete.description:
Revokes a pending invitation so that its token can no longer be redeemed.
Requires `iam.users.invite`, the same authority that issued it; a `CLIENT`
principal cannot hold the code and receives `404`. Revocation is a status
change, not a row deletion, so the record of who invited whom survives. An
invitation that has already been accepted cannot be revoked and is refused with
`409` — act on the resulting account instead. Success is `204`.

get.description:
Returns the whole permission catalogue: every code, the module it belongs to,
its principal-type envelope and whether it is classed as dangerous. Requires
`iam.permissions.read`, an `INTERNAL`-only permission, so a `CLIENT` caller sees
`404`. The catalogue is compiled into the binary rather than stored, so this is
a fixed list and not a paginated collection: there are no `cursor`, `limit` or
`sort` parameters. `max_principal_type: ANY` marks the only two codes a `CLIENT`
principal may ever hold, both of them `client.portal.*`.

Lists roles, cursor-paginated like every other collection in this API. Requires
`iam.roles.read` and no step-up; a `CLIENT` principal cannot hold the code and
is answered `404`. The projection is the role itself — read a role's grants with
`GET /api/v1/roles/{id}`. `sort` is allowlisted and an unlisted value is `400
VALIDATION_FAILED`, without the rejected string being echoed back.

post.description:
Creates a role together with its permission grants. Requires `iam.roles.create`
**and** step-up — `403 STEP_UP_REQUIRED` otherwise — because creating a role
creates authority; a `CLIENT` principal cannot hold the code and sees `404`. A
role is a reusable template and cannot name a specific object, so `RESOURCE`
scope is not expressible in `permissions`: the fields it would need are absent
from the type. The actor cannot grant a permission at a scope it does not itself
hold, and attempting to is `403 DELEGATION_DENIED`, while a code outside the
catalogue is `400 UNKNOWN_PERMISSION`. It honours `Idempotency-Key`, so a
retried create replays rather than duplicating.

get.summary: Read one role with its grants
get.description:
Reads one role together with its full grant list, which is what a reviewer needs
in order to see what the role actually confers. Requires `iam.roles.read` —
`INTERNAL` only, so a `CLIENT` caller sees `404` — and no step-up. An unknown id
is `404`. The `version` in the response is the optimistic-concurrency token a
subsequent `PATCH` must send back.

200.description: The role and its permission set.

patch.description:
Updates a role's name, description and permission set. Requires
`iam.roles.update` and step-up, since editing a role edits authority; a `CLIENT`
principal cannot hold the code and sees `404`. `code` and
`allowed_principal_type` are immutable here — the code is referenced by
operators and by seed data, and the principal type is the envelope the
permission set was authorised against, so a different envelope means a different
role. An absent `permissions` means leave the set alone, whereas an explicit
empty array is a legitimate instruction to strip the role bare; `version` is
mandatory and a stale one is `409 VERSION_CONFLICT`. Granting beyond the actor's
own authority is `403 DELEGATION_DENIED`.

delete.description:
Deletes a role outright. Requires `iam.roles.delete` and step-up; a `CLIENT`
principal cannot hold the code and receives `404`. A system role cannot be
deleted, and a role still assigned to anybody is refused with `409 ROLE_IN_USE`
rather than silently stripping its holders — revoke the assignments first.
Success is `204`.

get.summary: The roles assigned to a user
get.description:
Lists the roles currently assigned to one user. Requires `iam.roles.read` —
`INTERNAL` only, so an external caller sees `404` — and no step-up. It shows
assignments only; to see what those roles actually confer once overrides and the
principal envelope have been applied, use `GET /api/v1/users/{id}/permissions`.
An unknown subject id is `404`.

post.summary: Assign a role to a user
post.description:
Assigns a role to a user. Requires `iam.roles.assign`, which is classed as
dangerous and is therefore always behind step-up (`403 STEP_UP_REQUIRED`
otherwise); a `CLIENT` principal cannot hold it and sees `404`. It is refused
with `403 DELEGATION_DENIED` when the role carries authority the actor does not
itself hold, and with `409 PRINCIPAL_TYPE_MISMATCH` when the role's envelope
does not match the subject's — that second check is what stops a `CLIENT`
account ever acquiring an internal role. A successful assignment bumps the
subject's `security_version`, and because tokens are opaque server-side handles
rather than JWTs the new authority applies on the subject's very next request.

delete.summary: Revoke a role from a user
delete.description:
Removes a role assignment from a user. Requires `iam.roles.assign` — the same
dangerous permission that grants it — and is therefore behind step-up; a
`CLIENT` principal sees `404`. It bumps the subject's `security_version`, so the
reduced authority takes effect on their very next request and their clients can
detect that the capability set moved. Revoking an assignment that does not exist
is `404`; success is `204`.

get.description:
Returns a user's effective permissions: the union of role grants and direct
overrides, after the principal-type envelope has been applied and after any
`DENY` has won. Requires `iam.permissions.read` — `INTERNAL` only, so a `CLIENT`
caller sees `404` — and no step-up. This is a hint for user interfaces, exactly
like `capabilities` on `GET /api/v1/auth/me`: the backend re-derives every
decision per request regardless of what a client believes. An external subject's
list can only ever contain the two `client.portal.*` codes, which is asserted by
a property test over random grants.

get.summary: The permission overrides recorded against a user
get.description:
Lists the explicit permission overrides recorded against one user — the
exceptions that sit outside their roles, each with its effect, scope, reason and
the actor that granted it. Requires `iam.permissions.read` and deliberately
**not** `iam.permissions.delegate`, and it is not behind step-up: seeing which
exceptions exist is an inspection rather than a grant, so an auditor can be
given this read without also being handed the `POST` and `DELETE` on the same
path, both of which demand `iam.permissions.delegate` and a recent second
factor. A `CLIENT` principal can never hold the code and is answered `404`
rather than `403`. It returns the raw overrides and not the resolved picture;
for the union of role grants and overrides after the principal envelope has been
applied, use `GET /api/v1/users/{id}/permissions`. An unknown subject id is
`404`.

200.description: The overrides recorded against the subject.

post.summary: Grant or deny one permission directly to a user
post.description:
Grants or denies one permission directly to one user, bypassing roles. Requires
`iam.permissions.delegate`, a dangerous permission and therefore always behind
step-up; a `CLIENT` principal cannot hold it and sees `404`. The subject comes
from the path and never from the body, so the request cannot retarget a write
that the URL authorised. `resource_type` and `resource_id` are required with,
and only with, `RESOURCE` scope, and granting beyond the actor's own authority
is `403 DELEGATION_DENIED`. A `DENY` override beats every `ALLOW` from any
source, which makes it the reliable way to carve an exception out of a role.

delete.description:
Removes one permission override from a user. Requires `iam.permissions.delegate`
and is behind step-up, like every other delegation operation; a `CLIENT`
principal sees `404`. Removing an `ALLOW` withdraws that grant, whereas removing
a `DENY` restores whatever the role grants said — which *widens* the subject's
authority, so it is not the safe direction it appears to be. An unknown override
id is `404`; success is `204`.

get.description:
Lists departments, cursor-paginated and optionally filtered by `status`.
Requires `departments.read`, whose envelope is `INTERNAL`, so a `CLIENT`
principal is refused before any grant is consulted and is answered `404` rather
than `403` — an external principal must not learn that departments exist at all.
Departments are flat by design, so there is no tree to walk and no parent field.
`sort` is allowlisted and `limit` is bounded at 100.

post.description:
Creates a department. Requires `departments.create` — `INTERNAL` only, so an
external caller sees `404` — and no step-up. Departments are flat by design:
there is no parent, and no endpoint will ever nest one. A nominated
`lead_user_id` must be an `INTERNAL` principal, which the database enforces
rather than only the application layer, and a duplicate `code` is `409
UNIQUE_VIOLATION`. It honours `Idempotency-Key`, so a retried create replays
rather than duplicating.

get.description:
Reads one department by id. Requires `departments.read` — `INTERNAL` only, so a
`CLIENT` caller sees `404` — and no step-up. An unknown id is `404`, and for an
external caller a would-be `403` is rendered as `404` as well. The `version` in
the response is the optimistic-concurrency token a subsequent `PATCH` must echo.

patch.description:
Updates a department's name, description or lead. Requires `departments.update`
— `INTERNAL` only, so an external caller sees `404` — and no step-up. `code` is
immutable, and `lead_user_id` distinguishes absent, meaning leave the current
lead alone, from an explicit `null`, which detaches it. `version` is mandatory
and a stale one is `409 VERSION_CONFLICT` carrying the expected and actual
values.

post.description:
Archives a department. Requires `departments.archive` — `INTERNAL` only, so an
external caller sees `404` — together with the mandatory `version`. It is
refused with `409 DEPARTMENT_HAS_LIVE_PROJECTS` while any non-archived project
still belongs to it, so those projects must be moved or archived first. Archival
is terminal: there is no unarchive endpoint.

get.description:
Lists the live members of one department, cursor-paginated. Requires
`departments.read` — `INTERNAL` only, so a `CLIENT` caller sees `404` — and no
step-up. Live memberships only: removal sets `removed_at` and is recorded rather
than deleted, so history survives even though removed people do not appear here.
An unknown department id is `404`.

post.summary: Add a member to a department
post.description:
Adds a user to a department. Requires `departments.members.manage` — `INTERNAL`
only, so an external caller sees `404` — and no step-up. Only `INTERNAL`
principals may be members of an internal structure, and the database refuses
anything else even by direct SQL, so an attempt with a `CLIENT` subject is `409
INVARIANT_VIOLATION`. Adding somebody who is already a live member is `409
UNIQUE_VIOLATION`.

delete.summary: Remove a member from a department
delete.description:
Removes a member from a department. Requires `departments.members.manage` —
`INTERNAL` only, so a `CLIENT` caller sees `404` — and no step-up. It sets
`removed_at` rather than deleting the row, so the record that this person was
once a member survives and re-adding them later creates a new live membership.
Removing somebody who is not a live member is `404`; success is `204`.

get.description:
Lists client accounts — the external businesses the company works with — cursor-
paginated and optionally filtered by `status`. Requires `clients.read`, whose
envelope is `INTERNAL`, so a `CLIENT` principal is refused and answered `404`:
an external user must never be able to enumerate the company's other customers.
A client account is not a tenant, since there is one company and one database;
it is the visibility root that project shares hang from. `sort` is allowlisted
and `limit` is bounded at 100.

post.description:
Creates a client account representing an external business. Requires
`clients.create` — `INTERNAL` only, so an external caller sees `404` — and no
step-up. It is not a tenant: there is one company and one database, and the
named account manager is company staff and must therefore be an `INTERNAL`
principal. A duplicate `code` is `409 UNIQUE_VIOLATION`, and creating an account
grants nobody any visibility — that needs an activated member and an explicit
project share. It honours `Idempotency-Key`.

get.description:
Reads one client account by id. Requires `clients.read` — `INTERNAL` only, so a
`CLIENT` caller sees `404` even for its own account, because the portal is its
only surface — and no step-up. An unknown id is `404`. The `version` in the
response is the optimistic-concurrency token a subsequent `PATCH` must send
back.

patch.description:
Updates a client account's name, account manager or contact details. Requires
`clients.update` — `INTERNAL` only, so an external caller sees `404` — and no
step-up. `code` is immutable, because it is what operators and integrations
refer to. `version` is mandatory and a stale one is `409 VERSION_CONFLICT`; an
account manager who is not an `INTERNAL` principal is refused by the database.

post.description:
Archives a client account. Requires `clients.archive` — `INTERNAL` only, so an
external caller sees `404` — together with the mandatory `version`. Archiving
removes the visibility root: every project share that depended on an active
membership of this account stops resolving, so the external users attached to it
immediately see nothing in the portal. It is the fastest way to cut off an
external business wholesale, and it is terminal.

get.description:
Lists the external users attached to one client account, cursor-paginated.
Requires `clients.read` — `INTERNAL` only, so a `CLIENT` caller sees `404` — and
no step-up. Membership status is what matters: a `PENDING` membership is inert
and grants no visibility, an `ACTIVE` one is what makes project shares resolve,
and a `REMOVED` one is retained for history. An unknown client id is `404`.

post.summary: Attach an external user to a client account
post.description:
Attaches an external user to a client account. Requires `clients.members.manage`
— `INTERNAL` only, so an external caller sees `404` — and no step-up. Only a
`CLIENT` principal may be a member, and an `INTERNAL` subject is refused by a
database invariant rather than merely by application code. The membership is
created `PENDING` and is completely inert until it is activated, so this call by
itself exposes nothing; a duplicate live membership is `409`.

201.description: The membership was created, pending activation.

post.description:
Activates a `PENDING` client membership, which is the moment an external human
gains visibility of anything at all. Requires `clients.members.manage` —
`INTERNAL` only, so a `CLIENT` caller sees `404` — and no step-up. Until this
call the membership grants nothing; after it, every live project share on the
account resolves for that user. Activating a membership that is already
`ACTIVE`, or one that has been `REMOVED`, is `409`.

delete.summary: Remove a member from a client account
delete.description:
Removes an external user from a client account. Requires
`clients.members.manage` — `INTERNAL` only, so a `CLIENT` caller sees `404` —
and no step-up. It sets the membership to `REMOVED` rather than deleting it,
which withdraws every project the user could see through this account, with
effect on their next request. The user's own account is untouched: they can
still log in, they simply see nothing. Success is `204`.

get.description:
Lists projects, cursor-paginated and optionally filtered by `status` and
`department_id`. Requires `projects.read`, an `INTERNAL`-only permission, so a
`CLIENT` principal is refused and answered `404` — external users read projects
through `GET /api/v1/client-portal/projects`, which returns a smaller and
structurally different document. A narrow scope becomes a filtered query rather
than a refusal, so a caller with `ASSIGNED` scope sees only the projects they
are a member of. `sort` is allowlisted and `limit` is bounded at 100.

post.description:
Creates a project. Requires `projects.create` — `INTERNAL` only, so an external
caller sees `404` — and no step-up. The named manager must be an `INTERNAL`
principal, and a `target_date` earlier than the `start_date` is `400
VALIDATION_FAILED`. Creating a project shares it with nobody: external
visibility comes only from an explicit `POST /api/v1/projects/{id}/clients`,
which is itself behind step-up. It honours `Idempotency-Key`.

get.description:
Reads one project by id in the internal projection, including `internal_note`,
`manager_user_id`, `department_id` and `version`. Requires `projects.read` —
`INTERNAL` only, so a `CLIENT` caller sees `404` — and no step-up. External
principals reach projects only through the client portal, which returns
`ClientProjectResponse`: a structurally different and smaller type from which
those fields are physically absent rather than merely skipped during
serialisation. An unknown id is `404`.

patch.description:
Updates a project's mutable attributes. Requires `projects.update` — `INTERNAL`
only, so an external caller sees `404` — and no step-up. `code` is immutable and
`status` may not be set to `ARCHIVED` here, because archival has its own
endpoint so that it can carry a reason and its own audit action.
`department_id`, `start_date` and `target_date` distinguish absent, meaning
leave alone, from an explicit `null`, meaning clear. `version` is mandatory and
a stale one is `409 VERSION_CONFLICT`.

post.description:
Archives a project. Requires `projects.archive` — `INTERNAL` only, so an
external caller sees `404` — together with the mandatory `version`. Archival is
terminal, there being no unarchive endpoint, and existing client shares stop
resolving, so external users lose sight of it immediately. Archiving one that is
already archived is `409`.

get.description:
Lists a project's internal members, cursor-paginated. Requires `projects.read` —
`INTERNAL` only, so a `CLIENT` caller sees `404` — and no step-up. Company staff
only: client accounts with access appear under the project's client links, which
is a different relationship entirely and is read through `GET
/api/v1/projects/{id}/clients`. Removed members are retained with a `removed_at`
and are not listed.

post.summary: Add an internal member to a project
post.description:
Adds an internal member to a project. Requires `projects.members.manage` —
`INTERNAL` only, so an external caller sees `404` — and no step-up. Membership
is what resolves `ASSIGNED` scope for this project, so adding somebody genuinely
widens what that person can reach: it is an authorisation change dressed as an
ordinary write. Only `INTERNAL` principals may be members, anything else being
refused by a database invariant, and a duplicate live membership is `409`.

delete.summary: Remove an internal member from a project
delete.description:
Removes an internal member from a project. Requires `projects.members.manage` —
`INTERNAL` only, so a `CLIENT` caller sees `404` — and no step-up. It sets
`removed_at` and retains the row, and it narrows what the subject can reach
through `ASSIGNED` scope on their very next request. Removing somebody who is
not a live member is `404`; success is `204`.

get.summary: Which client accounts this project is shared with
get.description:
Lists the client accounts a project is currently shared with, cursor-paginated.
Requires `projects.read` — `INTERNAL` only, so a `CLIENT` caller sees `404` —
and no step-up. Live shares only: revocation is an update rather than a delete,
because the history of what was shared with whom is exactly what a client
dispute later turns on. An unknown project id is `404`.

200.description: A page of live client links.

post.summary: Share a project with a client account
post.description:
Shares a project with a client account, making it visible to every `ACTIVE`
member of that account. Requires `projects.clients.share`, which is classed as
dangerous and is therefore always behind step-up (`403 STEP_UP_REQUIRED`
otherwise) — this call crosses the external trust boundary, which is the whole
reason for the extra factor. A `CLIENT` principal cannot hold the code and is
answered `404`. It does **not** expose the project's tasks: task visibility is
per task, defaults to `false`, and is never inherited from the project. Sharing
with an account that already holds a live link is `409`.

201.description: The project is now visible to that client account.

delete.summary: Withdraw a project share from a client account
delete.description:
Withdraws a project share from a client account, so that its members stop seeing
the project on their next request. Requires `projects.clients.share` and is
behind step-up, exactly like the share it undoes; a `CLIENT` principal cannot
hold the code and sees `404`. It records the revocation rather than deleting the
link, so the history of what was shared with whom, and when it stopped,
survives. Revoking a link that is not live is `404`; success is `204`.

get.summary: List the tasks of one project
get.description:
Lists the tasks of one project, cursor-paginated and optionally filtered by
`status` and `priority`. Requires `tasks.read` — `INTERNAL` only, so a `CLIENT`
caller sees `404` — and no step-up. It returns the internal task projection,
including `internal_note` and `client_visible`; the external equivalent is `GET
/api/v1/client-portal/projects/{id}/tasks`, which returns a smaller type and
only the tasks explicitly marked visible. An unknown project id is `404`.

Lists tasks across every project the caller's scope reaches, cursor-paginated
and optionally filtered by `project_id`, `status` and `priority`. Requires
`tasks.read` — `INTERNAL` only, so an external caller sees `404` — and no step-
up. A narrow scope becomes a filtered query rather than a refusal, so a caller
with `ASSIGNED` scope sees only the tasks they are assigned to or whose project
they belong to. `sort` is allowlisted and `limit` is bounded at 100.

post.description:
Creates a task in a project. Requires `tasks.create` — `INTERNAL` only, so a
`CLIENT` caller sees `404` — and no step-up. `client_visible` defaults to
`false`: setting it true is the deliberate act that exposes a task to the client
portal, and it is never inherited from the project's share state. An unknown
`project_id` is `404`, and `Idempotency-Key` is honoured so that a retried
create replays rather than duplicating.

get.description:
Reads one task by id in the internal projection, including `internal_note` and
`client_visible`. Requires `tasks.read` — `INTERNAL` only, so a `CLIENT` caller
sees `404` and must use `GET /api/v1/client-portal/tasks/{id}` instead — and no
step-up. An unknown id, or one whose project is outside the caller's scope, is
`404` for an external caller and `403` for an internal one that lacks the
permission on an object which does exist. The `version` in the response is the
token a subsequent `PATCH` must send back.

patch.description:
Updates a task. Requires `tasks.update` — `INTERNAL` only, so an external caller
sees `404` — and no step-up. `project_id` is immutable: moving a task between
projects would move it across a visibility boundary silently, so it is not a
field of this request. `client_visible` *is* writable here, and flipping it to
true publishes the task to every client account the project is shared with.
`version` is mandatory and a stale one is `409 VERSION_CONFLICT`.

delete.description:
Deletes a task permanently. Requires `tasks.delete` — `INTERNAL` only, so a
`CLIENT` caller sees `404` — and no step-up. This is the only true delete in the
API and it is deliberately scoped to a task: users, projects, departments,
client accounts, invitations and audit rows are never deleted, only archived or
superseded. The deletion is itself audited, so the fact that a task existed and
was removed outlives the row. An unknown id is `404`; success is `204`.

get.summary: The internal users assigned to a task
get.description:
Lists the internal users currently assigned to one task, each with the actor
that assigned them and when. Requires `tasks.read` and deliberately **not**
`tasks.assign`: seeing who is assigned is part of reading the task, and
demanding the assignment permission to view the list would force every reader to
hold a write capability — it is the `POST` on this same path and the `DELETE` on
`/{user_id}` that require `tasks.assign`. Assignees are `INTERNAL` principals
only, enforced by a database trigger rather than by the handler, so the response
can never contain an external principal. A `CLIENT` principal cannot hold
`tasks.read` and is answered `404`, as is any caller for whom the task is not
visible, while an internal caller lacking the permission on a task that does
exist gets `403`. Live assignments only — removal sets `removed_at` and retains
the row — returned as a bounded array ordered by assignment time rather than as
a cursor page, because a task's assignee set is small.

post.summary: Assign an internal user to a task
post.description:
Assigns an internal user to a task. Requires `tasks.assign` — `INTERNAL` only,
so an external caller sees `404` — and no step-up. Assignees must be `INTERNAL`
principals, a `CLIENT` subject being refused by a database invariant, and
assignment resolves `ASSIGNED` scope for this task, so it widens what the
assignee can reach. Assigning somebody who is already a live assignee is `409`.

delete.summary: Unassign a user from a task
delete.description:
Unassigns a user from a task. Requires `tasks.assign` — the same permission that
assigns — and no step-up; a `CLIENT` principal cannot hold the code and sees
`404`. It sets `removed_at` and retains the row, so the record that this person
was once responsible survives. It narrows the subject's `ASSIGNED` scope on
their next request; unassigning somebody who is not a live assignee is `404` and
success is `204`.

get.summary: Projects shared with the caller's client accounts
get.description:
Lists the projects shared with the client accounts the caller belongs to — the
external principal's entry point, and one of only four routes a `CLIENT` may
reach. Requires `client.portal.projects.read`, which together with
`client.portal.tasks.read` is one of the only two codes whose envelope permits a
`CLIENT`; an `INTERNAL` principal granted the same code may also call it, but
will see nothing unless it happens to hold client memberships. Visibility is
derived entirely from data — a live project share joined to an `ACTIVE` client
membership joined to an `ACTIVE` client account — so possession of a project
UUID authorises nothing. Only `cursor` and `limit` are accepted: there is no
`sort`, no `direction` and no `department_id`, because an external principal
must not learn that departments exist.

Reads one shared project in the reduced client projection, from which
`internal_note`, `created_by`, `manager_user_id`, `department_id` and `version`
are physically absent rather than skipped during serialisation. Requires
`client.portal.projects.read` and no step-up; it is one of the four routes an
external `CLIENT` principal may reach. The row is fetched *with* the visibility
predicate, so a project that exists but is not shared with the caller produces
no row and therefore `404`, never `403` — a refusal must not confirm that the
identifier names something real. Tasks are not included; fetch them from `GET
/api/v1/client-portal/projects/{id}/tasks`.

get.summary: The client-visible tasks of a shared project
get.description:
Lists the client-visible tasks of a shared project, paginated with `cursor` and
`limit` only. Requires `client.portal.tasks.read` and no step-up; it is
reachable by an external `CLIENT` principal, which is the entire point of the
route. It returns only tasks explicitly marked `client_visible`: sharing a
project does not share its tasks, and visibility is never inherited. A project
that is not shared with the caller, or does not exist, is `404` rather than
`403`.

Reads one client-visible task in the reduced client projection, with
`internal_note` and the internal identifiers physically absent from the type.
Requires `client.portal.tasks.read` and no step-up; it is one of the four routes
an external `CLIENT` principal may reach. A task that is not marked
`client_visible`, or whose project is not shared with the caller, yields `404`
and never `403`, so the response cannot be used to probe which task ids are
real. There is no write endpoint anywhere in the portal: it is read-only by
construction, asserted by a test over the route table.

Returns every system setting with its current value, type and metadata. Requires
`settings.read` — `INTERNAL` only, so a `CLIENT` caller sees `404` — and no
step-up. It is a fixed catalogue rather than a paginated collection, so there
are no `cursor`, `limit` or `sort` parameters. `is_security_sensitive` marks the
settings whose modification is itself a security event, and those are the ones a
reviewer should watch for in the audit log.

put.description:
Writes the value of one system setting, identified by the key in the path.
Requires `settings.features.write` — `INTERNAL` only, so an external caller sees
`404` — and no step-up. The key is not a member of the body: a body that also
carried the key would let it retarget a write that the URL authorised.
`is_security_sensitive`, `value_type` and `description` are likewise not
writable, because being able to re-describe a setting is being able to pick
which permission guards it. `version` is mandatory and a stale one is `409
VERSION_CONFLICT`; an unknown key is `404`.

get.description:
Returns every feature flag together with whether it is currently enabled.
Requires `settings.read` — `INTERNAL` only, so a `CLIENT` caller sees `404` —
and no step-up. It is a fixed catalogue rather than a paginated collection, so
no `cursor`, `limit` or `sort` is accepted. A flag is a product switch and never
an access control: `client_portal = false` hides the portal, but it is the
`client.portal.*` permissions and the `CLIENT` envelope that actually stop an
external user reading a project.

put.summary: Turn one feature flag on or off
put.description:
Turns one feature flag on or off, identified by the key in the path. Requires
`settings.features.write` — `INTERNAL` only, so an external caller sees `404` —
and no step-up; the permission is deliberately not classed as dangerous, because
it is meant to be delegable to whoever runs the product. `version` is mandatory
for the same reason as on settings, a blind overwrite never being the default,
and a stale one is `409 VERSION_CONFLICT`. An unknown key is `404`, and the key
is never taken from the body.

get.summary: Minimal environment description for an authenticated client
get.description:
Returns a minimal description of the running environment: the environment name,
whether the system has been initialised, and the list of enabled feature keys.
Any authenticated session may call it, internal or external, and no permission
is required — which is exactly why it says so little. Deliberately absent are
build and version identifiers, the schema version, hostnames, the database, the
mail provider, pool statistics, uptime and the permission catalogue; each of
those would turn a routine authenticated read into reconnaissance for whoever
phishes one low-privilege account. `enabled_features` is a flat list of string
keys and never a list of objects.

Reads the audit log, cursor-paginated, with filters for `action_code`,
`actor_user_id`, `target_type`, `target_id`, `outcome` and an occurred-at range.
Requires `audit.read` — `INTERNAL` only, so a `CLIENT` caller sees `404` — and
no step-up. The log is read-only: there is no endpoint anywhere that writes,
edits, deletes or purges an audit event, and adding one would need an ADR rather
than a pull request. Each event carries its sequence number and chain hash,
which is what `GET /api/v1/audit/verify` recomputes.

parameters.name: action_code
parameters.description: Exact match on the action code, e.g. `ROLE.ASSIGNED`.

200.description: A page of audit events, newest first by default.

get.description:
Reads one audit event by id, including its sequence number, chain hash and the
structured detail recorded with it. Requires `audit.read` — `INTERNAL` only, so
a `CLIENT` caller sees `404` — and no step-up. An unknown id is `404`. There is
no way to modify what comes back, because audit history has no mutation path at
all.

Recomputes the HMAC-SHA256 hash chain over the requested `from_seq`–`to_seq`
range and reports the first sequence number at which it breaks, if any. Requires
`audit.read` **and** step-up, which is unusual for a `GET`: it mutates nothing,
but it is expensive enough to be a denial-of-service lever, and step-up is the
cheapest way to keep it out of casual reach. A `CLIENT` principal cannot hold
`audit.read` and is answered `404`. The claim this endpoint supports is precise
— modification, deletion or reordering performed without the chain key is
detectable — and it is not a claim of tamper-proofing against an adversary
holding both the database and the key. An invalid range is `400
VALIDATION_FAILED`.

parameters.name: from_seq
parameters.description: Inclusive lower bound on `seq`. Defaults to the first event.

parameters.name: to_seq
parameters.description: Inclusive upper bound on `seq`. Defaults to the latest event.

bearerAuth.description:
`Authorization: Bearer <token>` and nothing else. No cookies, no query
parameters, no custom headers, no basic auth.

**The token is an opaque server-side session token, not a JWT.** It has no
readable payload, no signature a client can verify and no claims: it is
random material whose only meaning is the row it selects in the session
store. Do not attempt to decode it, do not cache decisions derived from it,
and do not assume it will keep its current length. Server-side sessions are
used precisely so that revocation is immediate — a self-contained token
stays valid until it expires no matter what the server decides in the
meantime.

Access tokens are prefixed `rb_at_` and live 15 minutes; refresh tokens are
prefixed `rb_rt_`, rotate on every use and are single-use. Presenting an
already-redeemed refresh token is treated as theft and revokes the whole
session family.

**A token must never be placed in a URL** — not in the path, not in the
query string. URLs are written to proxy logs, kept in browser history and
forwarded in `Referer`. The server rejects any attempt to authenticate that
way; it is not a supported fallback. For the same reason the password-reset
and invitation-acceptance tokens travel in the request body.

XRequestId.description:
The request correlation id in force for this request. Echoed on every
response, present in every log line and stored on every audit row. Quote it
when reporting a failure.

Cursor.name: cursor
Cursor.description:
Opaque keyset cursor taken from `next_cursor` of the previous page. Opaque on
purpose: an encoded blob discourages hand-crafted cursors and lets the internal
representation change without breaking clients. It is **not** a security
boundary — it is not signed, and a forged cursor can only reposition a query
the caller was already authorised to run. A malformed cursor is
`400 VALIDATION_FAILED` with a field error on `cursor`.

Limit.name: limit
Limit.description:
Page size. Defaults to 25. A value below 1 or above 100 is
`400 VALIDATION_FAILED` with field code `OUT_OF_RANGE`; a deployment may
configure a lower cap, which a client cannot override.

Sort.name: sort
Sort.description:
The public name of a sortable field. Each endpoint has a compile-time
allowlist mapping a public name to a static SQL expression; the supplied
string is only ever compared, never interpolated. A value outside the
allowlist is `400 VALIDATION_FAILED` with field code `NOT_ALLOWED`, and the
error names the permitted set but never echoes what was rejected.

Direction.name: direction
Direction.description: Sort direction. Lowercase only; `ASC` is rejected.

XRequestId.name: X-Request-Id
XRequestId.description:
A client-supplied correlation id. **Accepted but not trusted**: it is used only
if it is 8–64 characters of ASCII alphanumerics, `-` and `_`. Anything else is
silently discarded and the server generates its own — a rejected value is not
an error. The adopted value is echoed on the response.

IdempotencyKey.name: Idempotency-Key
IdempotencyKey.description:
Makes this creation safely retryable. The key is scoped to
`(principal, operation, key)`, so one principal's key can never replay
another's response.

Replaying the same key with the same body returns the stored response
verbatim. Replaying it with a **different** body is `409
IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED`; a retry that arrives while the first is still in
flight is also `409`. Records are retained for 24 hours.

8–200 printable ASCII characters, no spaces and no control characters. A UUID
is a good choice.

BadRequest.description:
The request could not be understood or failed validation. `code` is
`VALIDATION_FAILED` (with an `errors` array), `BAD_REQUEST`, or
`UNKNOWN_PERMISSION` when the caller supplied a permission code outside the
catalogue. There is no `422` in this API.

Unauthorized.description:
`code: AUTHENTICATION_FAILED`. Deliberately undifferentiated: an unknown
account, a wrong password, an expired token, a revoked session, a malformed
bearer header and a suspended user all render identically, because any
distinction is an account-enumeration oracle.

Forbidden.description:
The caller is authenticated but the operation is refused. `code` is one of
`AUTHORIZATION_DENIED`, `STEP_UP_REQUIRED` (with a `step_up.window_seconds`
hint so the client re-prompts rather than gives up), `MFA_REQUIRED` when the
session has not completed its second factor, `DELEGATION_DENIED` when the
actor tried to grant authority it does not itself hold, or `ROOT_PROTECTED`
when the target was the system owner.

An external `CLIENT` principal receives `404` instead of this status wherever
a `403` would confirm that an object exists.

NotFound.description:
`code: RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND`. Also returned in place of `403` to external
principals, so that a refusal does not confirm the existence of an object they
should not know about.

Conflict.description:
The request conflicts with the current state. `code` is `VERSION_CONFLICT` for
stale optimistic concurrency, `IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED`,
`SYSTEM_ALREADY_INITIALIZED`, or one of the domain conflict codes such as
`UNIQUE_VIOLATION`, `EMAIL_IN_USE`, `ROLE_IN_USE` or
`DEPARTMENT_HAS_LIVE_PROJECTS`.

PayloadTooLarge.description: `code: PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE`. The body exceeds the accepted size and was not read.

UnsupportedMediaType.description: `code: UNSUPPORTED_MEDIA_TYPE`. Every body-bearing endpoint accepts `application/json` only.

RateLimited.description: `code: RATE_LIMITED`. `Retry-After` carries the wait in seconds.

InternalError.description:
`code: INTERNAL_ERROR`. The cause is logged against `request_id` and is never
returned. Quote `request_id` when reporting the failure.

ServiceUnavailable.description: `code: SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE`. A required dependency is unavailable; retry shortly. The failing dependency is never named.

FieldError.description: One rejected field inside a `VALIDATION_FAILED` problem.

field.description: Dotted path to the offending field, e.g. `name` or `members.0.user_id`.

code.description: Stable, machine-readable reason. Branch on this, not on `message`.

message.description:
Human hint. **Never echoes the rejected value** — echoing it back is how a
validation error becomes a reflection gadget and a log-injection vector.

Problem.description:
RFC 9457 problem details. Served as `application/problem+json` with
`Cache-Control: no-store`.

Two rules govern this shape. **Machine clients branch on `code`, never on
prose** — `title` and `detail` are human text and may be reworded at any time.
And **`detail` never carries an internal fact**: no SQL, no backtrace, no file
path, no environment variable, no secret, no database hostname. Internal causes
are logged against `request_id` and the client is told only that something
failed.

type.description:
`https://roleblank.internal/problems/<lowercased code>`. Deliberately not a
live URL: resolving it must never be required to handle an error, and
pointing at an external host would leak error occurrence to that host.

title.description: Short human summary. Not stable; do not match on it.

status.description: The HTTP status, repeated in the body.

code.description:
The stable contract identifier. The first eighteen values are the fixed
arms of the error type and are exhaustive for every status other than
`409`. `409` additionally carries a domain conflict code; the ones the
services construct today are listed after them.

detail.description: Client-safe explanation. Audited for information leakage.

request_id.description: Correlation id, matching the `X-Request-Id` response header.

window_seconds.description:
How recently the second factor must have been verified, in seconds.
Re-verify through the MFA endpoints and retry.

PageMeta.description:
The pagination envelope shared by every collection response. Keyset
pagination throughout: there is no `page`, no `offset` and no `total`. An
offset would let a client turn a cheap endpoint into an expensive one by
incrementing a number, and a total requires a second scan of the whole
matching set on every request.

next_cursor.description: Pass as `cursor` to fetch the next page. `null` on the last page.

PrincipalType.description:
The security envelope a human principal lives inside. Not a role and not
changeable by role assignment: it is fixed when the account is created and
caps the authority the account can ever hold, before any grant is consulted.

UserStatus.description: Account lifecycle. `ARCHIVED` is terminal; there is no delete.

ClientMembershipStatus.description: A membership grants visibility only while it is `ACTIVE`.

MembershipRole.description: Role within a department or project. Not a permission role.

ScopeType.description:
How wide a grant reaches. Five variants, no more. `RESOURCE` names one object
and is expressible only on a per-user override, never on a role: a role is a
reusable template and cannot name a specific object.

RoleScopeType.description: The four scopes a role grant may carry. `RESOURCE` is absent by design.

Effect.description: A `DENY` override beats every `ALLOW` from any source.

HealthResponse.description:
One field, and its value is one of two constants. There is deliberately no
`checks`, `details`, `version` or `error` member: a readiness body that names
the failing dependency tells an unauthenticated caller the shape of the
deployment.

environment.description: One of three fixed words. A client legitimately renders differently against a development instance.

initialized.description: Whether bootstrap has happened. Already observable anonymously, so disclosing it here costs nothing.

enabled_features.description: The feature-flag keys that are on. Keys only — never a description, never a sensitivity marker, never a value.

initialized.description:
`false` means bootstrap is still available. One boolean and deliberately
nothing else: version, hostname, user count or build id would each be free
reconnaissance handed to whoever finds the deployment first.

BootstrapRootRequest.description:
Four fields, and it cannot carry a fifth: unknown members are rejected before
the service is entered. `principal_type`, `status`, `is_root`, `mfa_required`,
`role_ids` and `security_version` are not fields of this request, so the
owner's security envelope cannot be chosen by the caller — it is written as
SQL literals.

bootstrap_secret.description:
The out-of-band operator secret, compared in constant time against the
deployment's configured value. Never logged, never audited, never echoed.

password.description: The owner's password. Never defaulted — a hardcoded owner credential would be a backdoor surviving every deployment of the image.

BootstrapRootResponse.description:
No token and no session. The owner must log in through the ordinary
authentication path and enrol a second factor, which is what makes bootstrap
incapable of minting a privileged session by itself.

mfa_enrolment_required.description: Always `true`. The owner is created with `mfa_required` set and no factor enrolled, so their first session can reach nothing but the MFA endpoints.

refresh_token.description: The `rb_rt_` token from a previous issue. Single use.

TokenResponse.description:
The single response shape for login, refresh and any other token issue. This is
the only place in the system where plaintext token material exists after
generation: it is serialised into the response and dropped.

access_token.description: Opaque session token, prefixed `rb_at_`. Send it in the `Authorization` header as a bearer credential. Never put it in a URL.

refresh_token.description: Opaque rotation token, prefixed `rb_rt_`. Single use; reuse revokes the session family.

expires_in.description: Lifetime of `access_token` in seconds — **not** of the session.

mfa_required.description:
`true` when this session may reach only the MFA endpoints and
`GET /api/v1/auth/me`. Complete a factor to clear it.

PasswordResetAccepted.description:
A fixed constant with no variable field. Identical for an existing account, a
non-existent account and a structurally invalid address — it is a struct with
nothing to vary precisely so that no future edit can make it depend on the
account.

token.description: The reset token from the email. In the body, never in the URL.

CodeRequest.description: A presented one-time code — TOTP for activation and verification, or a recovery code.

Capability.description: One permission the principal holds, with every scope it holds it at.

Me.description:
The full projection, returned to a session that has satisfied every
requirement. `capabilities` is a *hint* for hiding buttons; the backend
re-derives every decision on every request regardless of what the client
believes.

is_root.description: True only for the single system owner.

security_version.description: Bumped on every privilege change, so a client can see that its capability set moved.

step_up_active.description: Recomputed per request from the session's verification time. Never a stored flag — a cached boolean keeps saying "recently verified" after the window closes.

PendingMfaMe.description:
The reduced projection for a session that has not completed MFA. A
structurally smaller document rather than the full one with fields hidden: the
capability list must be *absent*, not merely omitted by an attribute a later
refactor could drop. A session that cannot call a business endpoint has no
business learning which business endpoints it would be allowed to call.
`is_root` and `auth_level` are absent for the same reason.

next_action.description: Which of the two MFA flows the client should start.

MeProjection.description: One of two structurally different documents. Discriminate on `mfa_pending`.

SessionSummary.description:
`id` is safe to expose: a session id is not a credential and the token digest
is not derivable from it.

current.description: Whether this is the session making the request.

absolute_expires_at.description: The ceiling. No amount of refreshing extends it.

client_ip_hint.description: Recognition aid only. Never used for authorisation.

user_agent_hint.description: Recognition aid only. Never used for authorisation.

TotpEnrolment.description:
The one response in this API that carries a secret, and it carries it exactly
once. `secret` and `otpauth_uri` are shown at setup and can never be read back,
because at rest the factor holds only authenticated ciphertext. Render the URI
as a QR code and discard it.

secret.description: Base32, no padding — what an authenticator app expects.

RecoveryCodes.description: Shown once. Only SHA-256 digests are stored, so they cannot be re-read.

mfa_required.description: Always `false` after a successful verification — the session is no longer restricted to the MFA endpoints.

recovery_codes_remaining.description: Present only on the recovery-code path, so a user can see the batch draining and regenerate before running out.

RegistrationConfig.description: Two fields and nothing more. It must not disclose the configured mode name.

registration_type.description: `client` when self-registration is on, `null` otherwise. Self-registration can only ever create a `CLIENT` principal.

RegisterRequest.description:
Three fields. There is no field for `principal_type`, none for `role_ids`, none
for `status`, and unknown members are rejected — mass assignment is refused by
the type, not by a service check somebody could forget to write.

RegistrationAccepted.description: A constant, byte for byte identical whether or not the address could be registered.

CreateInvitationRequest.description:
`department_id` is meaningful only for an `INTERNAL` invitation and
`client_account_id` only for a `CLIENT` one; the database refuses the other
combination outright.

role_ids.description: Roles to grant on acceptance. Validated against the inviter's own authority now, and again at acceptance.

Invitation.description: There is no field here the invitation token could occupy; it exists only in the email that was sent.

AcceptInvitationRequest.description: The token travels in the body, never in the path or the query string.

token.description: The `rb_iv_` token from the invitation email.

display_name.description: Optional override of the name the inviter supplied.

AcceptInvitationResponse.description: No session and no token. The new account must log in through the ordinary path.

User.description:
The internal user projection. `email_normalized` is deliberately absent, and
there is no field capable of holding a password hash — the hash lives in a
different table, so the query that runs on every authenticated request
physically cannot return one.

version.description: Optimistic-concurrency token. Send it back on any mutation.

max_principal_type.description: `INTERNAL` = internal principals only. `ANY` = a `CLIENT` may hold it, and only the `client.portal.*` codes are like that.

is_dangerous.description: Granting *or* exercising it requires a recent step-up.

PermissionCatalogue.description: The whole catalogue. It is compiled into the binary, so it is a fixed list rather than a paginated collection.

RolePermissionInput.description:
One `(permission, scope)` pair inside a role. There is deliberately no
`resource_type` or `resource_id`: a role cannot name a specific object, so the
fields a `RESOURCE` scope would need are physically absent rather than
validated away.

allowed_principal_type.description: Fixed at creation. Changing it later would move an existing permission set across the client envelope.

UpdateRoleRequest.description:
`code` and `allowed_principal_type` are absent on purpose and cannot be changed
here.

permissions.description:
Absent means "leave the permission set alone"; present means "replace it
with exactly this". An explicit empty array is a legitimate request to
strip the role bare.

RoleSummary.description:
Deliberately not closed with `additionalProperties: false`, because
`RoleDetail` composes it with `allOf`; a closed base would make that
composition unsatisfiable.

is_system.description: A system role cannot be deleted and its code is fixed by seed data.

AssignRoleRequest.description: The subject comes from the path, never from the body.

scopes.description: Every scope the subject effectively holds for this permission.

EffectivePermissions.description:
A hint for user interfaces, exactly like `capabilities` on the current
principal. The backend re-derives every decision per request regardless of
what a client believes.

CreateOverrideRequest.description:
`resource_type` and `resource_id` are required with, and only with, `RESOURCE`
scope. The subject is taken from the path.

expires_at.description: Must be in the future when present. A time-boxed override is preferable to a permanent one.

PermissionOverrideList.description:
The raw overrides for one subject. Not the resolved permission set —
`EffectivePermissions` is that, and it is what a user interface should read.

UpdateDepartmentRequest.description: `code` is immutable. An explicit `null` on `lead_user_id` detaches the lead; omitting the member leaves it alone.

Client.description: An external client business. Not a tenant — there is one company and one database.

account_manager_user_id.description: Company staff. Must be an `INTERNAL` principal.

status.description: `ARCHIVED` is not reachable here; archival has its own endpoint.

user_id.description: Must be a `CLIENT` principal. The membership starts `PENDING` and grants nothing until activated.

activated_at.description: When the membership became live. Until then it granted no visibility at all.

Project.description:
The **internal** project projection. Compare `ClientProject`, which is a
separate, smaller type rather than this one with fields filtered out.

UpdateProjectRequest.description: `code` is immutable and `status` may not be set to `ARCHIVED` here.

ShareProjectRequest.description:
There is deliberately no `tasks` and no `include_tasks` member: sharing a
project can never be a way to share its tasks.

Task.description:
The **internal** task projection. Compare `ClientTask`, which is a separate,
smaller type.

client_visible.description:
Per task, defaults to `false`, and **not** inherited from the project.
Sharing a project with a client must never silently expose its task list.
Setting this true is the deliberate act that exposes the task to the client portal.

UpdateTaskRequest.description: `project_id` is immutable: moving a task between projects would move it across a visibility boundary silently.

ClientProject.description:
The reduced project projection returned to an external `CLIENT` principal.

**The reduction is a security boundary, not a convenience.** This is a separate
type from `Project`, not the same document with fields filtered at
serialisation time: `internal_note`, `created_by`, `manager_user_id`,
`department_id` and `version` are physically absent, so there is no attribute,
no flag and no refactor that can make them appear. Filtering at serialisation
would leave the fields present in the type and one careless edit away from the
wire. `department_id` is withheld along with the rest because an external
principal must not learn that departments exist at all.

ClientTask.description:
The reduced task projection returned to an external `CLIENT` principal.

**The reduction is a security boundary, not a convenience.** Like
`ClientProject`, this is a separate type from `Task`: `internal_note`,
`created_by`, `client_visible`, assignee identities and `version` are
physically absent. A task reaches this projection only when it is explicitly
marked client-visible *and* its project is shared with a client account the
caller actively belongs to; `client_visible` itself is not echoed, because a
client has no use for a flag whose only false value it can never observe.

value.description: Validated against `value_type` before it is written.

is_security_sensitive.description: Marks a setting whose modification is itself a security event.

UpdateSettingRequest.description:
`key` is not a member: it comes from the path. A body that also carried the key
would let it silently retarget a URL-authorised write.

value.description: The new value. Validated against the stored `value_type`.

AuditEvent.description:
One row of the append-only log. `metadata` is a closed, sanitised structure
written by the server — never a raw request body. Passwords, tokens of any
kind, TOTP secrets, recovery codes and keys never appear in it.

seq.description:
Position in the hash chain. A gapless monotonic sequence, so "a row was
removed" is detectable on its own.

metadata.description: Sanitised, structured context for the event.

prev_hash.description: Hex-encoded 32-byte chain link of the previous entry. `null` for the first.

AuditVerification.description:
The result of recomputing the chain. `valid: false` with a `broken_at_seq`
means the log was modified, reordered or truncated without the chain key —
which is exactly the claim the chain supports, and no more.

broken_at_seq.description: The first sequence number at which the recomputed hash disagreed. `null` when `valid` is true.
